differentiation.extension: For pairs who finish early: instead of assuming q = Q/10, estimate q by modelling the paper as a disk of area A_paper = 1 cm^2 and the balloon as a sphere of radius R ≈ 0.10 m. Derive q ≈ Q (A_paper / (4π R^2)). Recompute Q and n using this area-based relation, show the algebra with units, and compare the result to the conservative q = Q/10 assumption; explain which gives a larger n and why.
differentiation.support: If a pair cannot start, pair them with a stronger partner and give this worked first item on the slip: Example work: m = 2.0×10^-5 kg, g = 9.8 m/s^2 so W = m g = 2.0×10^-5 kg × 9.8 m/s^2 = 1.96×10^-4 N. Use r = 0.02 m, k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2, assume q = Q/10 so k Q^2/(10 r^2) = W. Rearranged: Q^2 = 10 W r^2 / k. Plug numbers: Q^2 = 10 × (1.96×10^-4 N) × (0.02 m)^2 / (8.99×10^9) = compute this on calculator = 8.71×10^-21 C^2 so Q = 9.34×10^-11 C. Then n = Q / e = 9.34×10^-11 C / 1.60×10^-19 C = 5.8×10^8 (about 6×10^8 elementary charges). Use this as a template and replace numbers with your measured r and paper count.

materials: wool or nylon cloth (a small square of fabric per pair)
small scraps of paper (about 10 per pair, ~1 cm squares)
metric ruler (class set or one per pair)
printed data slip (one per pair) with value e = 1.60×10^-19 C and space for calculations
stopwatch or phone timer (one per pair)
student_instructions: 1) Inflate and tie your balloon to about 20 cm diameter. Start the stopwatch and rub the balloon with the fabric for 30 seconds. Write the rubbing time on your slip.

2) Place ~10 paper scraps on the desk. After rubbing, slowly bring the balloon toward the top paper and count how many papers are attracted and stick to the balloon. Record the count N_papers (unit: count). Do not let air currents move the papers.

3) Measure the closest distance r (in meters) from the balloon surface to the paper when attraction first occurs; record r with units (use cm and convert to m on your calculator). Record the mass per paper m = 0.02 g = 2.0×10^-5 kg (given).

4) Estimate a conservative lower bound for the balloon's net charge Q (in coulombs) as follows, showing every algebra step and units: (a) write the paper weight W = m g, with g = 9.8 m/s^2 and units N; (b) assume the electric force on one paper is F_e ≥ W; (c) use Coulomb's law F_e = k |Q q| / r^2 with k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2; (d) to avoid measuring q, assume q ≈ Q/10 (a conservative redistribution assumption) and substitute to get F_e ≈ k Q (Q/10) / r^2 = k Q^2/(10 r^2); (e) set k Q^2/(10 r^2) = W and solve step-by-step for Q (show algebra and units); (f) compute numerical Q in C, then compute n = Q / e and give n as an order-of-magnitude integer (include units: coulombs and number of elementary charges).
5) Write the final answers on the slip: rubbing time (s), N_papers (count), r (m), Q (C), and n (unitless count of e). Be ready to explain one algebra step to the teacher.
success_criteria: Each pair has a completed slip showing rubbing time (s), paper count (unit: count), measured r with units (m), and numerical values for Q in coulombs and n (unitless) with algebra steps visible.
While circulating you can see at least one pair carrying out the algebra on their calculator or paper with units carried through each step (e.g., kg·m/s^2 for weight, N·m^2/C^2 for k).
At least two students can point to the line on their slip where they set electric force ≥ weight (F_e ≥ mg) and used Coulomb's law to solve for Q.
teacher_instructions: 1) Organize students into pairs and give each pair the materials: 1 balloon, fabric, ~10 paper scraps, ruler, calculator, and one printed data slip. Tell them: 'You will charge a balloon, use it to lift papers, count how many elementary charges correspond to that measured charge, and show the derivation step by step.'

2) Demonstrate at the front: inflate a balloon (not fully; ~20 cm diameter), tie it, rub it with the fabric for 30 seconds, and bring it near a loose paper scrap to show attraction. Say: 'We measure how many papers are attracted; each attracted paper indicates a minimum net charge magnitude that can hold that paper against gravity for a short time.'

3) Start the 10-minute timer and instruct pairs to run the procedure on their slip: rub the balloon 30 s, bring it near the pile, count how many papers stick, measure the shortest distance at which the paper is attracted using the ruler, and record times and counts. While they work, circulate and check that pairs rub the balloon for 30 s, count visible attracted papers (not ones moved by air), and write numbers with units.

4) After data collection (about 5–6 minutes), instruct pairs to compute a lower-bound estimate of the balloon's net charge: (a) assume each paper has mass m ≈ 0.02 g (teacher-provided on slip) and that electrostatic attraction force at closest distance r must be at least equal to paper weight mg; (b) use Coulomb's law form F = k Q q / r^2 and treat q as one paper's induced charge, approximate q = Q (paper area / balloon area) is too detailed—instead derive a simple lower bound by assuming q ≈ Q/10 (explain this is conservative); (c) solve for Q in coulombs, then divide by e = 1.60×10^-19 C to get n. Pairs must show each algebra step and units on the slip.

5) End class by collecting one example slip from a pair and ask three pairs to read their final n value aloud. While students report, note any showing disappearance-of-charge misconception and correct it: emphasize conservation and redistribution of charge when objects touch, not destruction.
activities.title: Counting Charge on a Charged Balloon

differentiation.extension: Harder: Replace q2 in Problem 2 with a uniformly charged conducting rod of length 0.10 m centered at x = 0.30 m carrying total charge -2.0 nC. Derive an expression (with integral) for the x-component of the force on q3 due to the rod: set up the integral, carry units through, and evaluate numerically. State any approximations used.
differentiation.support: If stuck, use this sentence frame: “Coulomb’s law starts as F ∝ q1 q2 / r^2. Introducing k gives F = k·(q1 q2)/r^2 where k = 1/(4πε0) = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2. For Problem 2, convert: 4.0 nC = 4.0×10^-9 C. The distance r between a charge at x=a and x=b is r = |b−a| m.” Example worked first step: For q1 on q3, r = |0.20−0.00| = 0.20 m; q1 = 4.0×10^-9 C, q3 = 1.0×10^-9 C; substitute into F = k q1 q3 / r^2 and compute units N.

materials: textbook or reference with value of ε0 (optional)
student_instructions: General: Write every algebraic step, carry units through each calculation, and give final numeric answers with units. Use e = 1.60×10^-19 C and ε0 = 8.85×10^-12 C^2/(N·m^2).

Problem 1 — Conductor vs Insulator (qualitative, 3 min): You place a small metal sphere and a plastic sphere each carrying the same amount of excess negative charge. a) Describe where the excess electrons end up in the metal and draw a simple diagram showing charge distribution. b) Do the same for the plastic sphere (an insulator). c) State one experimental observation you would make that distinguishes the two (what you could see or measure).

Problem 2 — Superposition of Forces on a Test Charge (quantitative, 5 min): Three point charges lie on the x-axis: q1 = +4.0 nC at x = 0.00 m, q2 = -2.0 nC at x = 0.30 m, and a small test charge q3 = +1.0 nC at x = 0.20 m. a) Convert every charge from nC to C showing the multiplication by e.g. 1 nC = 1.0×10^-9 C. b) Write Coulomb’s law beginning from the proportionality F ∝ qA qB / r^2, then introduce k = 1/(4πε0) and substitute the numeric value and units for k. c) Calculate the force on q3 due to q1 (vector, with sign and units). Show magnitude, direction, and units. d) Calculate the force on q3 due to q2 (vector). e) Use vector superposition to find the net force on q3; show the vector sum step and the final numeric result with units.

Problem 3 — Charge Quantisation and Order-of-Magnitude (quantitative, 4 min): A small object has a net charge of q = -2.56×10^-17 C. a) Using q = n·e, compute n (the integer number of excess electrons) and state whether this n must be an integer; show your division and units. b) Give an order-of-magnitude statement: approximately how many electrons is that? Write the answer in the form n ≈ ? × 10^m electrons and show reasoning.
End: Box each final numeric answer and underline where you used (i) superposition, and (ii) q = n·e.
success_criteria: At least one student in each pair writes Coulomb’s law starting from F ∝ q1 q2 / r^2 and then substitutes k = 1/(4πε0) with numeric value and units.
Each pair calculates both pairwise forces in Problem 2, shows their directions on the x-axis, and writes the vector sum step to produce a single net force with units.
Each pair converts charges to coulombs and computes n in Problem 3, showing the division q/e and giving an integer or nearest-integer statement.
teacher_instructions: 1. Arrange students in pairs. Say: “You have 12 minutes to complete three numbered problems; write every step and unit. I will circulate and check units and arithmetic.”
2. Hand out or display the problems (student_instructions). Start the timer for 12 minutes.

3. While students work, circulate. For each pair, check that they (a) write the origin of Coulomb's law (proportionality then introduce k = 1/(4πε0)), (b) show vector addition for forces, and (c) convert between n (elementary charges) and q (coulombs) with units.

4. With 3 minutes remaining, announce time left and ask pairs to box their final numeric answers with units and underline the step where they used superposition and the step where they converted charges using q = n·e.
5. Collect papers or have pairs swap with another pair for quick peer check of units and arithmetic.
activities.title: Three Quick Problems: Conductors, Superposition, and Charge Quantisation

differentiation.extension: For an early-finisher: use the ruler measurement 2a = 20 cm and assume each rod carried charge magnitude q = 1.6×10^-6 C (use that number). Estimate the electric field magnitude at a point on the line perpendicular to the midpoint at a distance r = 50 cm from the midpoint (treat the pair as a dipole). Show the step-by-step vector sum of fields from each charge (include units N/C), then compute an approximate dipole moment p = q(2a) in coulomb·meter and express p in SI units.
differentiation.support: Pair a student who struggles with a student who explains observations. Give this sentence frame: “The source is _____ because ______. The test charge moved _____ at distance _____ cm, so the field there is toward/away from the source.” Work the conversion example together: q = 1.6×10^-6 C; e = 1.60×10^-19 C; n = q/e = (1.6×10^-6)/(1.60×10^-19) = 1.0×10^13 elementary charges.

materials: Two insulating rods or long plastic rulers (can be rubbed to charge) or one plastic rod and one glass/plastic ruler
Two different cloths for rubbing (e.g., wool and silk or fur and cloth)
A handful of small pieces of tissue paper (about 1 cm squares) or small bits of aluminum foil
Whiteboard and marker (or paper and pen) for short calculations
student_instructions: You are in a pair. Watch the teacher’s demonstration carefully and be ready to report three short observations to the teacher when asked.

During Part A (source vs test): note which object is the source and which is the test charge. Record at each distance (5 cm, 10 cm, 20 cm) whether the tissue paper is attracted, repelled, or not noticeably affected.

During Part B (superposition): at the midpoint between the two rods, say whether the paper feels a net leftward, net rightward, or nearly zero horizontal force. If there is movement when you nudge the paper left or right, describe which way it moves and why you think that shows vector addition of the two fields.

During Part C (flux and dipole): look at the small taped square area element. State the direction of the area vector (normal) the teacher used and say whether the electric flux through that square is positive, negative, or near zero when (i) only one rod is present and (ii) both rods form a dipole. Write down the short numerical conversion the teacher shows (compute n for q = 1.6×10^-6 C using e = 1.60×10^-19 C).
success_criteria: Each pair can identify which object in Part A was the source and which the test charge and can point to the distance where the test paper showed the strongest attraction.
At least one student in each pair can indicate the two individual force directions during Part B (arrows left and right) and can state the observed net direction at the midpoint.

Each pair can state whether the small taped square’s flux sign (positive/negative/near zero) changed when going from one rod to both rods and can point to the area vector direction used in the demonstration.
teacher_instructions: Group students in pairs. Tell the class: “You will watch a 12-minute demonstration and then each pair will answer two short questions on the worksheet. The demonstration shows (1) source vs test charge, (2) superposition of fields from two charges, (3) electric flux through a small flat surface, and (4) what we call an electric dipole.”

Prepare the two rods: rub one rod with one cloth and the other rod with the other cloth for 30 seconds each to give them opposite signs if materials are different (say plastic rubbed with wool becomes negative, glass with silk becomes positive). Place the rods on the table 40 cm apart, held by masking tape so they don’t roll. While rubbing, say aloud which rod you expect to be positive or negative and why (anchor to rubbing materials).

Demonstration part A — source and test charge (3 minutes): Hold one charged rod (source) stationary on the table. Pick up one small piece of tissue paper (test charge) with tweezers or fold it on a table and bring it slowly 5 cm from the rod. Ask a student pair to observe and report whether the tissue moves and in which direction. Repeat at 10 cm and 20 cm. While doing this, narrate: “The rod is the source charge; the paper is the test charge. We treat the rod as fixed so it defines the electric field.”

Demonstration part B — superposition (3 minutes): Place one charged rod at x = 0 cm and the other at x = 20 cm (use the ruler to measure). Hold a single folded tissue paper at x = 10 cm (midpoint) at a fixed height and ask two different pairs to watch. Bring the rods in, keeping both fixed, and show whether the paper is attracted, repelled, or sees competing forces. Move the paper slightly left or right and ask students to describe the net motion. Verbally model adding vectors: point left force from left rod and right force from right rod and add them.

Demonstration part C — flux and dipole geometry (4 minutes): Tape a small 2 cm × 2 cm square of paper (area = 4 cm^2 = 4×10^-4 m^2) to the ruler so it stands as a flat area element at the midpoint between the rods, with its normal vector pointing along the line joining the rods. Ask students to imagine field lines crossing this element. First, show when only one rod is present (remove the other): ask pairs to predict direction of E and whether E·A is positive or negative using E dA cosθ and state units (N·m^2/C). Then restore both rods (forming a dipole with charges ±q separated by 20 cm = 2a). Explain the dipole moment vector direction (from negative to positive) and point it out physically. Finally, ask: is net flux through this small square zero, positive, or negative? Use the idea that flux = E·dS and that for a small element near the midpoint the incoming and outgoing lines from the two charges will usually not cancel perfectly — ask one pair to give the observation and one pair to write the quick estimate on the board.

While the demonstration runs, circulate and ask each observed pair to state aloud: the sign of each rod, the direction of the test paper force, and whether the flux through the taped square is positive/negative/zero. After the demo, write on the board the quantisation relation q = n e and do one short numeric conversion: if q = 1.6×10^-6 C, how many elementary charges n = q/e? Show calculation and units on the board; ask a volunteer pair to perform the arithmetic (estimate acceptable).
activities.title: Hands-on: Two Charged Rods, One Test Paper — Superposition, Flux, Dipole

differentiation.extension: Change q to 1.0e−9 C and increase a to 0.10 m. Compute the dipole field at R = 5.0 m using both the exact numeric addition of two point-charge fields (sum fields from +q at +a and −q at −a) and the dipole approximation E_dip ≈ (1/(4πϵ0))·(2qa)/R^3. Report both values, compute the percentage difference, and explain why the approximation improves or worsens when R changes relative to a. Show all units and steps.
differentiation.support: If you are unsure how to start, use this worked first item: q = 5e = 5 × 1.60 × 10^−19 C = 8.00 × 10^−19 C. Monopole at r = 0.05 m: E = k|q|/r^2 = (8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2)(8.00×10^−19 C)/(0.05 m)^2 = calculate result and write N/C. Sentence frame for comparisons: “At R = ___ m, E_mono = ___ N/C and E_dip = ___ N/C. The ratio E_mono(R1)/E_mono(R2) = ___ ≈ (R2/R1)^2, while E_dip(R1)/E_dip(R2) = ___ ≈ (R2/R1)^3.” Pair lower-step student with one stronger peer if stuck.

materials: worksheet printed one per pair (see steps below)
stopwatch or timer visible to class
student_instructions: You are a pair. Use the calculator and show units at every step. Convert centimetres to metres when required (1 cm = 0.01 m). Use the elementary charge e = 1.60 × 10^−19 C and k = 8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2 (or 1/(4πϵ0)).
Step A — Charge conversion (2 minutes): Compute q in coulombs using q = n e with n = 5. Show q in C. (Example: q = 5 × 1.60 × 10^−19 C = ? C).

Step B — Monopole comparison (3 minutes): Treat a single +q at the origin. Compute the electric field magnitude E_mono at r1 = 0.05 m, r2 = 0.15 m, and r3 = 0.50 m using Coulomb’s law E = k|q|/r^2. Write each E with units N/C and record ratios E(r1)/E(r2) and E(r2)/E(r3).

Step C — Dipole approximation (3 minutes): Model a dipole formed by +q at x = +a and −q at x = −a with a = 0.01 m. For points on the x-axis at distances R = 0.05 m, 0.15 m, and 0.50 m from the origin (R >> a), compute the approximate dipole field magnitude using the leading-order far-field expression derived from Coulomb’s law for two charges: E_dip ≈ (1/(4πϵ0))·(2qa)/R^3. Derive this form briefly by adding the fields from +q and −q along the axis and keeping the first nonzero term in a/R. Use p = q(2a) and write E_dip in N/C. Record the ratios E_dip(R1)/E_dip(R2) and E_dip(R2)/E_dip(R3).

Step D — Compare fall-off (1 minute): Compare the numerical ratios from Steps B and C and state which falls off faster with R (1/R^2 vs 1/R^3). Give one numerical example (a ratio) to support your statement.

Step E — Gauss’s law check (1 minute): Imagine a spherical surface of radius 0.02 m centered at the origin. Decide whether the total enclosed charge is zero or nonzero for (i) the monopole case where only +q at origin exists, and (ii) the dipole case with +q and −q at ±a. Use Φ = Q_enclosed/ϵ0 to compute the flux Φ in each case and give units (N·m^2/C).
success_criteria: Each pair shows q in coulombs with correct multiplication by e and correct units (e.g. q = 8.00 × 10^−19 C).

Each pair writes three monopole E values with units N/C and three dipole E_dip values with units N/C, and can point to the ratio demonstrating a 1/R^2 versus 1/R^3 trend (monopole ratios ≈ (R2/R1)^2, dipole ratios ≈ (R2/R1)^3).
Each pair correctly states the enclosed charge and writes the numerical flux Φ with units N·m^2/C for the sphere examples.
teacher_instructions: 1. Arrange students in pairs. Hand each pair the printed worksheet that lists the numerical scenario: a point charge +q and a point charge −q separated by 2a = 2.0 cm (so a = 1.0 cm), with q = 5e (five elementary charges). Tell students they have 10 minutes and start the timer. Say: “We will compute fields at three distances, compare fall-off rates, check flux through a sphere, and convert charge units.”

2. Tell pairs to follow the worksheet step sequence. While they work, circulate and check units are carried (e.g. distances in metres, charge in coulombs). If a pair finishes early, give them the extension question on the whiteboard. If a pair is stuck on starting values, read the worked example in the Support aloud once.

3. After 8 minutes announce: “Prepare one clear sentence stating whether the dipole field falls faster than the monopole and give one numerical ratio you found.” Call on two pairs to read their sentence and ratio in 30 seconds each. Record one pair’s computed flux value on the board.

4. At the end of 10 minutes collect the worksheets and note pairs that used correct unit conversions and who produced the numerical comparisons. Do not lecture; use student answers to plan next class.
activities.title: Desk Simulation: Compare Monopole and Dipole Fields, Flux, and Charge Quantisation

differentiation.extension: Harder task: Change q2 to +1.0 μC (both positive) and place them at x=0 and x=0.30 m. (a) Find the location(s) on the x-axis where E = 0; show algebraic steps and units. (b) For the original signs (+2.0 μC and −1.0 μC), estimate the net force on a small dipole (p = 4.0×10^-29 C·m) placed at x = 0.15 m if the field there has a small gradient dE/dx = 1.0×10^6 N/(C·m). State whether a net force exists and compute its approximate magnitude using F ≈ (p·dE/dx).
differentiation.support: If you are stuck on Prompt A, use this sentence frame to start: "Field at the mid-point = field from q1 (magnitude __ N/C to the right/left) plus field from q2 (magnitude __ N/C to the right/left)." Worked first lines for A: distance from each charge to mid-point = 0.15 m. Compute E1 = k·|q1|/r^2 = (8.99×10^9)(2.0×10^-6)/(0.15^2) N/C; compute E2 similarly with q2 = 1.0×10^-6 C.

materials: marker for each pair (or one per student)
handout with three numbered prompts (one per pair) — teacher can write prompts on board instead
student_instructions: You will work through three short physics prompts. For each prompt: first think alone and write your answer with numbers and units; then explain your reasoning to your partner and listen to theirs.

Prompt A — Two point charges: q1 = +2.0 μC at x = 0 and q2 = -1.0 μC at x = 0.30 m. Find the electric field vector E at the point x = 0.15 m (midway). Show steps: compute magnitude of field due to each charge using Coulomb’s law E = k|q|/r^2 (use k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2), give each field a direction (left or right along x), then add the two vectors and show final magnitude with unit N/C and direction.

Prompt B — Field lines and flux: On the supplied small square patch (drawn at x = 0.15 m, side = 0.05 m, normal along +x), draw the expected field lines from the two charges above. Then compute the electric flux through the square approximately by treating E as constant across the patch: flux = E_x · area, where area = (0.05 m)^2 and E_x is the x-component of the net field at the patch. State units (N·m^2/C) and explain whether you would draw more or fewer lines to represent relative strength (and why that does or does not change physical field).

Prompt C — Dipole torque: Imagine a permanent dipole with dipole moment magnitude p = 4.0 ×10^-29 C·m oriented at 60° to a uniform electric field E = 2.0×10^5 N/C. Derive the torque magnitude by starting from τ = pE sinθ (explain where this comes from as magnitude of p cross E), calculate the numerical value in N·m, state the direction of torque (tends to rotate dipole to align p with E), and comment whether a net force exists when E is uniform versus when E varies in space.
success_criteria: At least one student in each pair writes numerical values with appropriate units for magnitude of E in Prompt A and points to the directions on their sketch.
Pairs draw field lines for Prompt B that start on + charges and end on − charges and compute a flux value showing area (m^2) times E_x (N/C) giving N·m^2/C.
Pairs performing Prompt C write the torque computation showing τ = pE sinθ, give a numeric torque in N·m, and state aloud that net force is zero in a uniform field but nonzero in a non-uniform field.
teacher_instructions: 1) Arrange students in pairs. Tell groups they will do three short tasks: (A) field from two point charges, (B) field lines and flux through a small patch, (C) dipole in a uniform field. Display or read the three prompts and start a 3-minute individual think time for prompt A.

2) After 3 minutes, say “Pair up and explain your answer for A to your partner” and start a 2-minute paired-explain timer. Circulate: check each student writes numbers with units, points to vector directions, and is using vector addition for fields; if a pair is stuck, read the scaffold sentence in Support aloud to one student.

3) Repeat the same cycle for prompts B and C: 3 minutes individual thinking, 2 minutes paired explanation for B; then 3 minutes individual thinking, 2 minutes paired explanation for C. While pairs talk, listen to one pair per round and write a short correction on the board if a common error appears (for example, crossing lines or misidentifying start/end of lines).

4) Bring the class together for the final 1 minute: call for one quick pair to state their result for each prompt (A, B, C). Correct any persistent errors and explicitly surface the two misconceptions listed: (a) number of drawn field lines is a drawing choice, not intrinsic; (b) induced polarization can produce attraction without net charge transfer.
activities.title: Quick Field, Flux and Dipole Reasoning

differentiation.extension: Compute the electric field at a point on the perpendicular bisector of a finite straight rod of length 2L and uniform linear charge density λ by integrating Coulomb’s law. Set up the integral using dq = λ dx, evaluate E_z at a distance z from the midpoint, carry units through, and show the limiting form as L → ∞ reproduces E = λ/(2π ε0 z).
differentiation.support: If you are stuck, start with the sentence frame: 'Choose symmetry -> Gaussian surface = ______. Only these faces contribute because ______. Flux = E·(contributing area) = ______. Q_enclosed = ______. Apply Gauss: E·(area) = Q_enclosed/ε0 -> solve for E.' Example worked first item (plane): Choose symmetry -> plane symmetry, Gaussian surface = pillbox. Only top and bottom faces contribute because E is normal and constant on these faces. Flux = E·A + E·A = 2EA. Q_enclosed = σA (σ in C/m^2). Gauss: 2EA = σA/ε0 -> cancel A -> E = σ/(2ε0) (units check: [σ]=C/m^2, [ε0]=C^2/(N·m^2) so [E]=N/C).

materials: printed 1-page worksheet per pair (one copy per pair; teacher can print in 5 minutes)
small round object to represent a spherical shell (ping-pong ball or small rubber ball) and a sheet of paper to represent an infinite plane
a straight object about 20–30 cm long to represent an infinite line (a pen or pencil)
student_instructions: You work in pairs. Use the printed worksheet and the classroom objects to draw the Gaussian surface, write the flux integral as Φ = ∮ E·dA, write the enclosed charge, and derive E step by step. Always write units next to each physical quantity.
Task A — Infinite line (use the straight object to imagine the charged wire):
1. Sketch a cylinder of radius r and length L coaxial with the line. Label r (m) and L (m).
2. Write the flux through the cylinder: only the curved surface contributes. Flux = E(r) · (curved area) = E(r) · (2π r L). Include units: E in N/C, area in m^2.

3. Write enclosed charge: Q_enclosed = λ · L where λ has units C/m. Substitute into Gauss’s law Φ = Q_enclosed/ε0 and solve for E(r). Show algebra that leads to E(r) = λ/(2π ε0 r) and write units for both sides.
Task B — Infinite plane (use the sheet of paper to imagine the charged plane):
1. Sketch a cylindrical pillbox that crosses the plane, with face area A (m^2). Label normal directions.
2. Write flux: flux = E_top·A + E_bottom·A = 2 E A (both faces). Include units.
3. Write enclosed charge: Q_enclosed = σ · A where σ has units C/m^2. Use Gauss’s law and solve for E = σ/(2 ε0). Show units.
Task C — Thin spherical shell (use the small ball to represent the shell):
1. Sketch two Gaussian spheres: one with radius r > R (outside), one with r < R (inside). Label R (m), r (m).
2. For r > R: write flux = E · (4π r^2). Enclosed charge Q = total shell charge Q (C). Use Gauss’s law to get E = Q/(4π ε0 r^2). Write units.
3. For r < R: state Q_enclosed = 0 so flux = 0 and E = 0. Explain in one sentence why this follows from symmetry.
Final small task (on worksheet): for each final formula, state the direction of E with words (radial outward/inward or normal to plane) and list the units of every symbol used (λ, σ, Q, r, ε0).
success_criteria: Each pair has a sketched Gaussian surface for each case (cylinder for line, pillbox for plane, sphere for shell) on their worksheet.

When asked, each pair points to the algebraic step where they substitute Q_enclosed into Gauss’s law and cancel common area or length (e.g., cancel A in the plane case, cancel L only where appropriate in line case).
Each pair writes units next to λ, σ, Q, r and shows units on the derived expression (e.g., shows that λ/(2π ε0 r) yields N/C).
teacher_instructions: 1. Arrange students in pairs. Hand each pair the printed worksheet and one ruler, one pen, one small round object, one straight object and one sheet of paper. items.stem: Two point charges lie on the x-axis: q1 = +3.0 μC at x = 0.00 m and q2 = −5.0 μC at x = +0.40 m. Using Coulomb's law with k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2, calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force on q1 due to q2 and give its direction (specify along +x or −x, or ‘towards q2/away from q2’).
items.working:
Step 1 — Write Coulomb's law for magnitude: F = k |q1 q2| / r^2.
Step 2 — Substitute numbers (convert μC to C): q1 = 3.0×10^−6 C, q2 = 5.0×10^−6 C (use absolute value for magnitude). r = 0.40 m.
Calculate product of charges: |q1 q2| = (3.0×10^−6 C)(5.0×10^−6 C) = 15.0×10^−12 C^2 = 1.50×10^−11 C^2.
Compute numerator k|q1 q2|: (8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2)(1.50×10^−11 C^2) = 8.99×1.50×10^(9−11) N·m^2 = 13.485×10^−2 N·m^2 = 0.13485 N·m^2.
Compute r^2: (0.40 m)^2 = 0.1600 m^2.
Divide to get force magnitude: F = 0.13485 N·m^2 / 0.1600 m^2 = 0.8428 N ≈ 8.4×10^−1 N (0.84 N).
Step 3 — Determine direction: q1 is positive and q2 is negative, so the force is attractive; q1 is pulled toward q2 which lies at +x. Therefore the force on q1 is along +x (to the right), i.e. towards q2.

items.answer:
(a) Infinite plane sheet, surface charge density σ:
Gaussian surface: a short cylindrical pillbox with flat faces parallel to the plane and equal area A, symmetric about the plane. Symmetry/justification: the plane is infinite and uniform, so E is perpendicular to the plane and has the same magnitude on both sides; flux only through the two flat faces. Field: E = σ/(2ε0) directed normal to the plane on each side.

(b) Infinitely long straight wire, linear charge density λ:
Gaussian surface: a coaxial cylindrical surface of radius r and length L. Symmetry/justification: translational and cylindrical symmetry imply E is radial, same magnitude at all points at distance r, and perpendicular to curved surface; no flux through end caps. Field: E(r) = λ/(2π ε0 r) directed radially outward (or inward if λ<0).

(c) Thin uniformly charged spherical shell radius R, total charge q:
Gaussian surface: concentric spherical surfaces of radius r. Symmetry/justification: spherical symmetry makes E radial and same at all points on a sphere. For r > R (outside): enclosed charge = q, so E(r) = q/(4π ε0 r^2) directed radially outward. For r < R (inside): enclosed charge = 0, so E = 0.

items.answer:
(a) The electric dipole moment vector p has magnitude p = q × 2a and points from the negative charge (−q) to the positive charge (+q). (1 mark)

(b) Each charge experiences a force F = qE (direction depends on sign). The forces on +q and −q are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction if the field is uniform, but because they act at different positions they produce a torque. The torque on the dipole about its centre can be written as the cross product
τ = p × E.

Magnitude: |τ| = p E sinθ = (2aq) E sinθ.

Vector/direction: τ is perpendicular to the plane containing p and E; using the right-hand rule for p × E, point fingers along p (from −q to +q), curl toward E; the thumb gives the direction of τ. (3 marks)

(c) In a uniform electric field the net force on the dipole is zero because the forces on +q and −q are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction and their vector sum cancels. However, in a non-uniform (spatially varying) electric field the magnitudes of the forces on the two charges will differ, producing a net force on the dipole. For a small dipole in a slowly varying field this net force is approximately (p · ∇)E (i.e. depends on the gradient of the field).

Addressing the misconception: attraction of a neutral object to a charged object (for example paper to a comb) does not mean the neutral object gained net charge. The neutral object can become polarized (an induced dipole): charges shift slightly inside it so that near-side induced opposite charge experiences a stronger attraction than the farther-side repulsion, producing net attraction without any net charge transfer. (2 marks)

items.answer: (a) Number of excess electrons on the charged sphere: n = q / (−e) = (−4.80 × 10−19 C) / (−1.602 × 10−19 C) = 2.995 ≈ 3 electrons. So the sphere has 3 excess electrons. (b) Total charge is conserved and equals −4.80 × 10−19 C. After touching two identical spheres, charge is shared equally, so charge on each = (−4.80 × 10−19 C) / 2 = −2.40 × 10−19 C. Number of excess electrons on each (approximate) = (−2.40 × 10−19 C) / (−1.602 × 10−19 C) = 1.498 ≈ 1.5 electrons. Because charge is quantised in whole electrons, in reality one sphere would have 2 excess electrons and the other 1 excess electron (total 3 electrons), but the equal sharing calculation gives −2.40 × 10−19 C per sphere (about 1.5 electrons each) as the ideal continuous result.

items.stem: A small insulating sphere carries a net charge of −4.80 × 10−19 C. (a) Calculate the number of excess electrons on the sphere. (b) The sphere is then touched to an identical neutral conducting sphere and the two spheres are separated. Calculate the final charge on each sphere and the (approximate) number of excess electrons on each. Use the elementary charge magnitude e = 1.602 × 10−19 C. Show units and steps.
items.working:
(a) Given q = −4.80 × 10−19 C and e = 1.602 × 10−19 C (magnitude of electron charge).
Compute number of excess electrons n:
n = q / (−e) = (−4.80 × 10−19 C) / (−1.602 × 10−19 C)
First divide magnitudes: 4.80 / 1.602 = 2.995 (unitless).
So n = 2.995 ≈ 3 electrons. Units: electrons (count).

(b) Conservation of charge: total Q_total = −4.80 × 10−19 C.
Two identical spheres share charge equally, so charge on each Q_final = Q_total / 2 = (−4.80 × 10−19 C) / 2 = −2.40 × 10−19 C (per sphere).
Number of excess electrons on each (approximate, using continuous division): n_each = Q_final / (−e) = (−2.40 × 10−19 C) / (−1.602 × 10−19 C) = 2.40 / 1.602 = 1.498 ≈ 1.5 electrons.
Note on quantisation: electrons are discrete, so the actual integer distribution consistent with total 3 electrons is one sphere with 2 electrons and the other with 1 electron, giving charges −3.204 × 10−19 C and −1.602 × 10−19 C respectively; the equal-sharing (−2.40 × 10−19 C each) is the ideal continuous result.

items.answer: A conductor is a material in which valence electrons (or charge carriers) can move freely through the material; an insulator is a material in which electrons are tightly bound to atoms and cannot move freely. When a solid conducting sphere receives extra electrons, the electrons move freely and redistribute themselves over the outer surface of the sphere until electrostatic equilibrium is reached; there is no excess charge left in the interior and the electric field inside the conductor is zero. By contrast, when a solid insulating rod receives extra electrons (for example by rubbing), the extra electrons stay localized near the region where they were placed and do not move freely to the whole surface; the charge remains stuck in that part of the insulator. An everyday example of a conductor is copper (used for electrical wiring because it allows current to flow easily). An everyday example of an insulator is plastic (used to coat wires and make handles because it prevents charge flow).

items.answer: Option 1: +Q is the source that produces the electric field and +q is the small test charge that experiences force F = qE; +q must be small or fixed so it does not disturb +Q, ensuring the measured field is that of +Q alone.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Correct. The source charge +Q creates the field; the test charge +q probes it by feeling a force F = qE. To define the field of +Q, +q must be small or fixed so it does not significantly alter +Q or the field configuration.
options.text: +Q is the source charge that produces the electric field; +q is the test charge that experiences the force. +q must be small (or fixed so it does not disturb +Q) so the field being measured is that of +Q alone.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Wrong: this implies the test charge and source are interchangeable and that the field is dominated by +q because of proximity. The test charge should be negligible so it does not produce a comparable field; the measured field is that due to +Q, not +q.
options.text: Both +Q and +q are equally source charges that produce separate electric fields; the measured field at a point is just the field of +q at that point because it is closer.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Wrong: a test charge need not be zero; it must be small enough that its own field is negligible. Taking q -> 0 is a limiting concept for defining E = F/q, but physically we use a small nonzero q that does not disturb the source.
options.text: A test charge must be exactly zero to avoid changing the field; therefore +q should be taken to zero for the electric field of +Q to exist.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Wrong: the electric field is a property of the source charge(s) and space, not of the test charge. The test charge experiences the field (force F = qE); it does not 'have' the field being measured.
options.text: The electric field is a property of the test charge +q and is measured by observing how +Q moves in response to +q.

items.stem: A fixed charge +Q sits at the origin and creates an electric field. A small positive test charge +q is brought close to +Q to measure the field. Which statement correctly describes the roles of +Q and +q when defining the electric field of +Q?

items.answer:
Sketch: Field lines start at the positive charge (+q) and end at the negative charge (−q); lines are more curved near the space between the charges and symmetric in a dipole shape. Arrows point away from +q and toward −q.

Three properties (one per letter):
(a) Direction: The tangent to a field line at any point gives the direction of the electric field there, so arrows point away from the positive charge and toward the negative charge.
(b) Spacing (density): The local density of field lines represents the relative magnitude of the electric field; where lines are closer together the field is stronger, and where they are farther apart the field is weaker.

items.stem: Two point charges +q and −q are placed on the x-axis at x = +a and x = −a respectively. Find an expression for the electric field magnitude E on the +x-axis at a point x = r where r >> a. Using a binomial expansion to first order in a/r, show that the field falls off as 1/r^3 and express your result in terms of the dipole moment p = q(2a). State the direction of the field. (4 marks)
items.working:
1. Exact fields from each charge at point x = r (r > a):
   E+ from +q at x = +a points in +x direction with magnitude E+ = (1/4πε0) q / (r − a)^2.
   E− from −q at x = −a points in +x direction (since −q attracts a positive test charge toward −x, but located at −a gives field at r directed toward −a, i.e. −x; however because the charge is negative the field at r is toward −a which is in the −x direction; careful: using signs explicitly below gives correct net direction).
2. Use algebra with signed fields (taking +x direction positive):
   Field from +q: E+ = (1/4πε0) q / (r − a)^2 (positive).
   Field from −q: distance to −q is r + a, and field points toward −q, i.e. in the −x direction, so E− = −(1/4πε0) q / (r + a)^2.
   Net field: E = E+ + E− = (1/4πε0) q [1/(r − a)^2 − 1/(r + a)^2].
3. Combine the difference of squares:
   1/(r − a)^2 − 1/(r + a)^2 = [(r + a)^2 − (r − a)^2] / [(r − a)^2 (r + a)^2]
   Numerator: (r^2 + 2ar + a^2) − (r^2 − 2ar + a^2) = 4ar.
   So the difference = 4ar / [(r − a)^2 (r + a)^2].
   Thus E = (1/4πε0) q (4ar) / [(r − a)^2 (r + a)^2].
4. For r >> a, approximate (r ± a)^2 ≈ r^2(1 ± a/r)^2 ≈ r^2(1 ± 2a/r) to first order, but product (r − a)^2(r + a)^2 ≈ (r^2 − a^2)^2 ≈ r^4 (1 − a^2/r^2)^2 ≈ r^4 to leading order. Therefore to leading order
   E ≈ (1/4πε0) q (4ar) / r^4 = (1/4πε0) (4qa) / r^3.
5. Write in terms of the dipole moment p = q(2a): then 4qa = 2p, so
   E ≈ (1/4πε0) (2p) / r^3.
6. Direction: the sign of E found above is positive, so the field is along +x (away from the dipole on the positive axis). Units are N C−1, showing the field scales as 1/r^3.

(End of working.)

Step 1 — write Coulomb's law (magnitude): F = k |q1 q2| / r^2, where k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2·C^−2.
Step 2 — substitute values with units: q1 = 3.0×10^−6 C, q2 = −2.0×10^−6 C (use absolute value for magnitude), r = 0.50 m.

items.stem: A thin straight rod of length L lies on the x-axis from x = 0 to x = L and carries a uniform positive linear charge density λ (C m–1). Find the electric field vector E at point P on the x-axis located at x = −a (a > 0). Give the magnitude and direction of E in terms of λ, L, a and the constant k = 1/(4πϵ0).
items.working:
Take an element of length dx at position x (0 ≤ x ≤ L) carrying charge dq = λ dx (units C). The position of P is x_P = −a. The separation from dq to P is r = x − (−a) = x + a (units m). The contribution to the electric field at P from dq, using Coulomb's law, is dE = k dq / r^2, directed from dq toward P (for positive λ the field points from the positive charge toward P, i.e. in the +x direction because dq is to the right of P). The field contributions are all along the x-axis, so vector signs reduce to a sign for the x-component. Using +x as the direction from P toward the rod, dE_x = k (λ dx)/(x + a)^2.
Integrate over the rod from x = 0 to x = L:
E_x = ∫_{0}^{L} k λ (dx)/(x + a)^2.
Compute the integral: let u = x + a, du = dx, limits u = a to u = a + L.
E_x = k λ ∫_{u=a}^{a+L} u^{-2} du = k λ [−u^{-1}]_{a}^{a+L} = k λ (1/a − 1/(a + L)).
Units check: k (N m^2 C^{-2}) × λ (C m^{-1}) × (1/m) gives N C^{-1} = V m^{-1}, correct for electric field.
Therefore E = E_x ˆi = k λ (1/a − 1/(a + L)) ˆi, pointing in the +x direction for positive λ.

items.stem: A single point charge Q = +5.0 μC is fixed at the origin. Calculate the electric field vector at the point P located at x = +0.20 m on the x-axis. Give the magnitude (in N C^-1) and the direction. (Take k = 8.99 × 10^9 N m^2 C^-2.)
items.working:
1. Write the electric field from a point charge: E = kQ / r^2, directed radially away from a positive charge.
2. Substitute values: Q = +5.0 μC = 5.0 × 10^-6 C, r = 0.20 m, k = 8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2·C^-2.
   E = (8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2·C^-2) × (5.0 × 10^-6 C) / (0.20 m)^2.
3. Calculate denominator: (0.20 m)^2 = 0.0400 m^2.
   Numerator: (8.99 × 10^9) × (5.0 × 10^-6) = 44.95 × 10^3 = 4.495 × 10^4 (units: N·m^2·C^-1).
4. E = (4.495 × 10^4) / 0.0400 N C^-1 = 1.12375 × 10^6 N C^-1.
5. Round to three significant figures (given data to three s.f.): E = 1.12 × 10^6 N C^-1.
6. Direction: Q is positive, so the electric field at P (x = +0.20 m) points away from the charge, i.e. in the +x direction.
Final answer: E = 1.12 × 10^6 N C^-1, directed along +x.

items.answer:
(a) Electric field magnitude: E = kQ/r^2 = (8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2)(5.0×10^-6 C)/(0.20 m)^2 = 1.12×10^6 N/C.

(b) Electric force on q: F = qE = (1.0×10^-9 C)(1.12×10^6 N/C) = 1.12×10^-3 N, directed radially outward from the source charge (repulsive since both charges are positive).

(c) The charge q is called a test charge because it probes the electric field produced by the source charge Q without significantly altering that field. q should be small compared with Q so that its own field does not appreciably move or change the source charge Q or the field configuration; this ensures the field measured depends only on the source charge.

rubric.criteria: Correct calculation of field and force; correct direction; clear explanation of why q is a test charge and must be small.

levels.descriptor: All parts correct: (a) E computed correctly with units and correct numeric value ≈ 1.12×10^6 N/C; (b) F computed correctly with units and correct numeric value ≈ 1.12×10^-3 N and direction stated as radially outward (repulsive); (c) concise correct explanation that q probes the field, defined by E = F/q, and q must be small so it does not appreciably alter the source charge or the field.
levels.label: Full marks

levels.descriptor: One computational part incorrect or missing but the other computation correct, and a partially correct explanation given (mentions that q probes the field or that it should be small but without linking to not altering the source/field). Example: correct E but wrong arithmetic in F (or vice versa), or correct numbers but missing units or slightly wrong by a factor of 2.5 or less.
levels.label: Partial credit

levels.descriptor: Major errors in computations (orders of magnitude wrong), wrong direction, and no or incorrect explanation about the role and required smallness of the test charge.
levels.label: No credit

items.stem:
A point source charge Q = +5.0 μC is fixed at the origin. (a) Calculate the electric field magnitude produced by Q at a distance r = 0.20 m from the origin. (b) A test charge q = +1.0 nC is placed at that location. Calculate the electric force on q and state its direction. (c) Briefly explain why q is called a test charge and why its magnitude should be small compared with Q when defining the electric field.

(Use k = 8.99 × 10^9 N·m^2/C^2. Show all steps and include units.)
items.working:
(a) Compute E from a point charge formula, showing units stepwise:
Q = 5.0 μC = 5.0×10^-6 C
r = 0.20 m
k = 8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2
E = kQ/r^2
  = (8.99×10^9 N·m^2/C^2) × (5.0×10^-6 C) / (0.20 m)^2
  = (8.99×10^9 × 5.0×10^-6) / 0.04  N/C
  = (8.99×5.0×10^3) / 0.04  N/C     [since 10^9 × 10^-6 = 10^3]
  = (44.95×10^3) / 0.04  N/C
  = 1.12375×10^6 N/C ≈ 1.12×10^6 N/C.

(b) q = 1.0 nC = 1.0×10^-9 C
F = qE = (1.0×10^-9 C)(1.12375×10^6 N/C)
  = 1.12375×10^-3 N ≈ 1.12×10^-3 N.
Direction: Both Q and q are positive, so the Coulomb force is repulsive; the force on q is radially outward from the origin.

(c) Explanation: The electric field E is defined as the force per unit test charge (E = F/q) produced by the source charge Q. To measure or define this field without changing it, the test charge q must be small so that its own electric field and the force it exerts on the source charge are negligible; otherwise the presence of q would alter the field that we aim to measure.

items.answer:
a) |E_P| : |E_Q| = 2 : 1 (i.e. |E_P| = 2|E_Q|).

b) The density of field lines leaving a charge represents the relative field strength; since A has twice as many lines leaving as B and the points are the same distance r, the field at P is twice that at Q. The absolute number of drawn field lines is not a fixed physical property — the artist can choose how many lines to draw, so only the relative density (lines per unit area around the charge) indicates relative field strength.

levels.label: Full credit

levels.label: Partial credit

items.stem:
Two isolated positive point charges, A and B, are drawn with field-line diagrams. Around charge A eight equally spaced field lines leave the charge; around charge B four equally spaced field lines leave the charge. Point P is at distance r from charge A along one of its field lines. Point Q is at the same distance r from charge B along one of its field lines. (a) Calculate the ratio of the magnitudes of the electric fields |E_P| : |E_Q| at P and Q. (b) Give a brief physical explanation (one or two sentences) that justifies this ratio and addresses whether the absolute number of drawn field lines is a fixed physical property of the charge.

(Mark allocation: 2 marks for the numeric ratio, 2 marks for the explanation.)
items.working:
Step 1: Use the rule that, in field-line diagrams, the local field magnitude is proportional to the local density of field lines (lines per unit area through a surface around the charge).

Step 2: At the same radial distance r, and along a single field line, the local density around A is proportional to the number of lines leaving A (8) and around B proportional to the number leaving B (4), assuming equal spacing.

Step 3: Ratio |E_P|/|E_Q| = (number of lines from A)/(number of lines from B) = 8/4 = 2.

Therefore |E_P| : |E_Q| = 2 : 1, so |E_P| = 2|E_Q|.

Units: electric field in newtons per coulomb (N C^-1), but ratio is dimensionless.

Emphasize units: 'Charge measured in coulombs.' Finally ask: 'Which would let charges move to the outside when charged, conductor or insulator?' Confirm: conductor.

anticipated_questions: Why use a positive test charge? (A positive test charge gives the direction of the field in the usual sense; if you used a negative test charge the force would be opposite.)
What does 'without disturbing the source charges' mean? (The test charge must be small enough that it does not change the arrangement of the source charges.)
Is electric field a vector? (Yes — magnitude and direction matter; we showed direction 'to the right'.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the operational definition exactly as given. Then write the numeric worked example: 'Given: F = 6.0×10^-3 N on q_t = 2.0 μC (2.0×10^-6 C). E = F / q_t = 6.0×10^-3 N ÷ 2.0×10^-6 C = 3.0×10^3 N/C (direction: right).' Include units N/C.
teacher_script.heading: Operational definition: electric field
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: 'Now we define electric field by an experiment.' Place an imagined small positive test charge q_t at a point P near a source charge +Q. Ask: 'What do we measure there?' Guide students to say 'a force on the test charge.' State the operational definition exactly: 'The electric field at a point is the force experienced by a unit positive test charge placed there (without disturbing the source charges); equivalently, force per unit test charge.' Now place numbers: 'If a 2.0 μC test charge experiences a force of 6.0 × 10^-3 N to the right at P, what is the field at P?' Pause for calculation. Lead them through: E = F / q_t, show units: N / C. Compute: 6.0 × 10^-3 N ÷ 2.0 × 10^-6 C = 3.0 × 10^3 N/C to the right. Emphasize 'unit positive test charge' and 'without disturbing the source charges' by asking what would happen if the test charge were large (it would change the source charges — not allowed for the definition).

anticipated_questions: Why can we just add forces? (Because electrostatic forces follow the superposition principle; each pairwise force is calculated as if other charges were not present.)
Do we need vectors? (Yes — direction matters; if forces are opposite we subtract magnitudes.)
What if the charges are not pointlike? (Today's examples use point-like or small localized charges; distribution issues come later.)
teacher_script.board_action: Draw the diagram with +Q1, +Q2, and q_t. Write bullet: 'Superposition: F_net = F_1 + F_2 (vector sum).' Then write the numeric steps showing q values in coulombs (convert using n·e in words), the given pairwise forces, the sum, and E_net = F_net / q_t with the final number and units N/C.
teacher_script.heading: Introduce superposition for forces and link to field
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Draw two source charges on the board: +Q1 at left and +Q2 at right, and a small positive test charge q_t at a point between them. Ask: 'What is the net force on q_t?' Let students suggest 'add the forces from each charge.' Say: 'That is the principle of superposition: the net electrostatic force equals the vector sum of the forces from each source, and each pairwise force is unchanged by the others.' Work one simple numeric example: Q1 = +2e (so compute in coulombs), Q2 = +1e, place q_t = +1e at a point where force magnitudes from each are 4.8×10^-20 N left and 2.4×10^-20 N right respectively (use these numbers). Ask students to compute net force and direction: net = 4.8×10^-20 N left minus 2.4×10^-20 N right = 2.4×10^-20 N left. Then show how to get net field by dividing net force by q_t: E_net = F_net / q_t — here q_t = 1e = 1.60×10^-19 C — compute E_net in N/C with units. Do the arithmetic aloud and write each step; keep units visible.

anticipated_questions: How did you get 3.2×10^-19 C for 2e? (Multiply 2 × 1.60×10^-19 C.)
Why is the field smaller than the force? (Because field is force divided by the test charge; large test charge gives smaller E for same F.)
Why is the sign negative for -5e? (Negative means an excess of electrons; the numerical value with sign gives direction for forces on positive test charges.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the two-part questions and leave space for student answers. After presentations, write the correct answers with calculation lines: '-5e = -8.0×10^-19 C' and 'E = F/q = 1.6×10^-19 N ÷ 3.2×10^-19 C = 0.50 N/C upward' (showing q = 2e = 3.20×10^-19 C).
teacher_script.heading: Guided practice: compute charge and field
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Give a quick two-part pair task (2 minutes): Part A: Convert -5e to coulombs. Part B: A test charge of +2e feels a force of 1.6×10^-19 N upward. What is the field at that point? Tell pairs: 'Write answers and one line of calculation; I'll call on two pairs.' Circulate, correct notation and units. Call on one pair to present both answers. If they make arithmetic slip, write corrected steps on the board and ask class to spot the mistake.

anticipated_questions: Will we need to memorize e exactly? (Yes — use 1.60×10^-19 C here; more precision not needed for these problems.)
How do we know when to divide by q to get E versus summing fields? (You can divide the net force by q or sum the fields from each source; both give the same E.)
teacher_script.board_action: Underline the main points already on the board. Add one final bullet: 'Takeaway: q in C (use n·e); E = F/q (N/C); superposition = vector sum; conductors: surface; insulators: localized.'
teacher_script.heading: Check for understanding and consolidate
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Ask two quick checks aloud: 1) 'If a conductor is charged, where will excess charges end up?' Students answer: 'on the surface.' 2) 'If two charges both push a test charge, how do we find the total force?' Students: 'Add the vector forces (superposition).' Summarize: 'We used q = n e to get coulombs, defined E = F/q operationally, and used superposition to get net force or field. Next period we will treat source vs test charge more formally and compute flux.' End by asking students to keep today's board notes in their notebook.

bullet_points: Electric field (operational): force on a unit positive test charge placed at the point (without disturbing the source charges); equivalently, force per unit test charge. Units: N/C.
Superposition: E_net = vector sum of fields from each source charge evaluated at the point.
Flux through element: dΦ = E · dS = E dS cosθ (θ = angle between E and area normal). Units: N·m^2/C.
Dipole: two equal and opposite point charges ±q separated by 2a. Dipole moment p = q 2a, directed from -q to +q. Units: C·m.
Quantisation: q = n e. Use e = 1.6×10^-19 C for calculations.
diagrams_to_draw: Point source charge (label +Q) with a small positive test charge at a nearby point; arrow showing force on test charge.
Two point charges on x-axis: +2.0×10^-6 C at x=-0.10 m and -1.0×10^-6 C at x=+0.10 m. Show field vectors at origin and arrows indicating directions.
Tiny surface element dS (square) with area normal arrow; show E making 60° with normal and the projection E cosθ through the area.
Dipole: -q at left, +q at right, separation labelled 2a; arrow from -q to +q labelled p.

They add in the +x direction, so the net E points +x. (Student should note both contributions point same way and add.)

checkpoint_questions.question: A dipole consists of +2.0e and -2.0e separated by 1.0 cm (so 2a = 1.0 cm). Give the dipole moment magnitude in coulomb·meter and state its direction using the definition in the lesson.

mentor_moment.story: I once rubbed a plastic comb and watched tiny bits of paper jump up. The comb didn't give the paper a net charge; the comb's field pulled the paper's charges slightly apart (an induced dipole), and the nearer opposite charges felt a stronger pull, so the paper stuck.
mentor_moment.takeaway: A neutral object can be attracted without net charging: induced dipoles in a non-uniform field produce a net force toward the charged object.
mentor_moment.title: Comb, paper and induced dipoles

Pause for 1 quick student answer. Then say: "If you wrote B, say how the charges are arranged in the paper." Pause for 1 quick answer. anticipated_questions: How small must a test charge be?
If the test charge moves, does it change the field?

teacher_script.board_action: Write the operational definition sentence exactly from the source and below it write units: E = N/C.
teacher_script.heading: Operational definition of electric field and source/test charges
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "We need a clear definition: place a tiny positive test charge at a point and measure the force on it without moving the source charges. The electric field is that force per unit positive charge." Put a small toy ball labelled +q_test and a larger fixed charged object on the desk as a physical anchor. Ask: "Which is the source charge and which is the test charge here?" Wait for answer. Then say: "The source charge must be treated as fixed; we only measure how a tiny test charge would feel a force there." Emphasize units: "Force in newtons divided by charge in coulombs gives E in newtons per coulomb (N/C)."

anticipated_questions: Why did both fields point the same way when one charge is negative?
Where did the value k = 9.0×10^9 come from?
What if the point wasn't on the line between charges?
teacher_script.board_action: Draw the two point charges with coordinates and arrows showing each field at the origin. Write the numerical calculation lines with k = 9.0×10^9 N·m^2/C^2 and show E1 = 1.8×10^6 N/C, E2 = 9.0×10^5 N/C, E_net = 2.7×10^6 N/C to the right.
teacher_script.heading: Superposition principle (vector sum of fields)
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "If there are several point source charges, the net electric field at a point is the vector sum of the fields each source would produce there. We'll do a quick two-charge example." Draw two point charges on the board: +2e-6 C at x = -0.10 m and -1e-6 C at x = +0.10 m. Ask: "At the origin, what is the direction of the field from each charge?" Pause for answers: left / right. Then compute magnitudes step by step: show Coulomb's law verbally: 'force ~ 1/r^2' but do not write new formulas beyond allowed. Use numeric values: distance from each to origin is 0.10 m; compute E1 = k*2e-6/(0.10^2) and E2 = k*1e-6/(0.10^2). Use k = 9.0×10^9 N·m^2/C^2 and show units. Calculate numbers: E1 = (9.0e9*2e-6)/(0.01) = (18e3)/0.01? Wait compute: 9e9*2e-6 = 18e3 = 1.8e4; divide by 0.01 gives 1.8e6 N/C. Similarly E2 = 9e9*1e-6/0.01 = 9e3/0.01 = 9e5? Check: 9e9*1e-6 = 9e3 = 9000; /0.01 = 900000 = 9e5 N/C. So net field is E_net = E1 (to right because + charge repels positive test?) Wait sign careful: At origin, +2e-6 at left (-0.1) pushes positive test to right. -1e-6 at +0.1 attracts positive test to right as well. Both to right, so add magnitudes: 1.8e6 + 9e5 = 2.7e6 N/C to the right. Say each arithmetic step aloud and write short lines of the computation, keeping units. Ask: "What does superposition mean here?" Summarize: "Vector add component-wise if not collinear."

anticipated_questions: What are the units of flux?
What does negative flux mean physically?
How small must dS be for this formula to be valid?
teacher_script.board_action: Write the flux formula exactly: dΦ = E · dS = E dS cosθ. Draw the surface element with normal, draw E at 60°, and show the numeric substitution and arithmetic leading to dΦ = 2.0 N·m^2/C.
teacher_script.heading: Introduce electric flux through a surface element
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Flux tells us how many field lines pass through a surface. For a tiny surface element dS, flux dΦ = E · dS = E dS cosθ where θ is angle between E and the area normal." Point to the board formula. Draw a small square surface element with a normal arrow and a field vector at an angle. Ask: "If E is parallel to the normal, what is cosθ and what is the flux sign?" Wait for 'cosθ = 1, flux positive'. Ask: "If E is perpendicular to the normal?" Wait for 'flux zero.' Then do a quick numerical example: choose E = 2.0×10^4 N/C, area dS = 2.0×10^-4 m^2, θ = 60°. Compute dΦ = E dS cos60° = 2.0×10^4 * 2.0×10^-4 * 0.5. Do arithmetic aloud: 2.0×10^4 * 2.0×10^-4 = 4.0×10^0 = 4.0; times 0.5 = 2.0. So dΦ = 2.0 (units: N·m^2/C). Write units explicitly. Emphasize interpretation: "Positive flux means field leaves through the surface in the direction of the area normal."

anticipated_questions: Why point from negative to positive, not the other way?
Is p a vector? What if charges are vertical?
How does induced dipole strength depend on the material?
teacher_script.board_action: Write the dipole definition sentence exactly and the formula p = q 2a. Under it write the numerical steps: q = 3×1.6×10^-19 = 4.8×10^-19 C; p = 4.8×10^-19 × 2.0×10^-9 = 9.6×10^-28 C·m. Draw a dipole diagram: -q at left, +q at right, arrow labelled p pointing right.
teacher_script.heading: Define electric dipole and quick calculation using quantisation q = n e
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "A dipole is two equal and opposite point charges +q and -q separated by 2a. The dipole moment p = q×2a and points from negative to positive." Point to the board definition. Give a concrete example: let q = 3 e (three elementary charges). Ask: "What is q in coulombs?" Wait for a student to say multiply by e = 1.6×10^-19 C. Do it: q = 3 × 1.6×10^-19 C = 4.8×10^-19 C. Next choose 2a = 2.0×10^-9 m (separation). Compute magnitude p = q×2a = 4.8×10^-19 C × 2.0×10^-9 m = 9.6×10^-28 C·m. Write units. Emphasize direction arrow from - to +. Ask: "Why does a neutral object stuck to a charged comb not require net charge?" Link back to induced dipole: one side slightly more negative than the other so the comb attracts it. If time, demonstrate with small pieces of paper and a charged comb (safety permitting).

anticipated_questions: Why did we pick the test charge positive in the definition?
Can flux be larger than the field value times area?
teacher_script.board_action: Write the two worksheet questions on the board. After students work, write the solutions: q = 1×1.6×10^-19 = 1.6×10^-19 C; p = q×0.10 = 1.6×10^-20 C·m. Flux = E dS cos0 = 5.0×10^3 × 1.0×10^-4 = 0.50 N·m^2/C.
teacher_script.heading: Guided practice and rapid consolidation
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Hand out a 2-question worksheet (or display on the board): (1) A point -1e charges at x=0.05 m and +1e at x=0.05 m; find q in C and p if separation 2a = 0.10 m. (2) A small surface element has area 1.0×10^-4 m^2, E = 5.0×10^3 N/C perpendicular to the surface normal. Compute flux. Give students 4 minutes to work and circulate. After 4 minutes, call the class back and write the answers step-by-step on the board, asking students to tell the next arithmetic step. End with: "What is one thing you will remember from today?" Have 1-2 students answer briefly.

anticipated_questions: Will we have homework on this?
Will we calculate dipole fields in detail next time?
teacher_script.board_action: Write two final prompts: 'Define dipole moment (one sentence)' and 'Units of flux and dipole moment'.
teacher_script.heading: Exit check and link to next lesson
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Quick check: in one sentence, what is the dipole moment and what are its units?" Call on 2 students. Then say: "Next time we'll compare how dipole fields fall off with distance compared to single charges and begin Gauss's law applications. Tonight, read the first paragraph on dipole field fall-off if you can." Collect any remaining worksheets as students leave.

bullet_points: Dipole: two opposite charges +q and −q separated by 2a, center at origin.
For point on axis at x = r with r >> a, distances: R+ = r − a, R− = r + a (units: m).
Add point-charge fields and expand in a/r to leading order: E ∝ p/(4πϵ0 r^3) with p = q(2a) (p in C·m).
Dipole field falls off as 1/r^3 for r >> a (not 1/r^2).
Coulomb's law (point charges): F = (1/4πϵ0) (q1 q2 / r^2) r̂  (N, C, m).
Gauss's law (integral): Φ_E = ∮ E · dS = q_enc / ϵ0.
Infinite line charge example: choose cylinder coaxial with line. Flux through curved surface = E(2π r L). Enclosed q = λ L.
Solve: E = λ/(2πϵ0 r) (units: λ in C/m, E in N/C).
Charge quantisation: q = n e, with e = 1.60×10^-19 C. Example: 20e = 3.20×10^-18 C.

Diagram: cylindrical Gaussian surface around an infinite line-charge (show radius r and length L).
Small table of sensor readings vs distance for demo (r = 5 cm, 10 cm, 20 cm) with ratios.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Dipole field scales as 1/r^3 so E2 = E1 × (r1/r2)^3 = 2.0×10^-6 N/C × (1.0/2.0)^3 = 2.0×10^-6 N/C × 1/8 = 2.5×10^-7 N/C. Units remain N/C.
checkpoint_questions.question: At points far from a dipole (distance r much larger than dipole half-separation a), the dipole electric field scales roughly as 1/r^3. Suppose at r = 1.0 m the field magnitude is E1 = 2.0 × 10^-6 N/C. Estimate the field at r = 2.0 m and show the reasoning with units.

Where did the 4a come from in the numerator?
